A2.text:
Tural is nineteen. He plays the tar — a traditional Azerbaijani instrument. He lives in an old building in Baku. Every afternoon, he sits near the window to rehearse for his music school exam.

Last month, a new neighbour moved into the flat upstairs. His name is Emin, and he makes electronic music on his computer. It is a very different genre. Tural's father did not like the loud beats. “That boy is tone-deaf!” he said.

One hot Tuesday, both windows were open. Tural was playing an old melody. Upstairs, Emin heard it and started a slow drum beat. At first, Tural stopped. Then he smiled and played the chorus again. For twenty minutes, they played together through the open windows.

That evening, Emin knocked on Tural's door. “That was music to my ears,” he said. “What if we try a real collaboration?”

They wrote a song together, without any lyrics, and practised all week. On Sunday, they gave a small live performance in the courtyard for the neighbours. Tural was nervous — it was time to face the music, especially in front of his father.

When the song ended, everyone clapped. Even Tural's father smiled and had to change your tune — “All right,” he said, “that was actually good.”

B1.text:
In the old stone courtyard where Tural lives, everyone hears everything. So when Tural sat by his open window each afternoon to rehearse on the tar for his conservatory exam, the whole building knew every note of his programme.

Nobody minded until June, when a twenty-four-year-old producer named Emin moved into the flat above. Emin's genre was electronic music, and his bass lines shook the teacups in Tural's kitchen. Tural's father was furious. “The boy is completely tone-deaf,” he grumbled at dinner. “It's just noise — no lyrics, no soul.”

One windless afternoon, Tural was working through a slow folk melody when a soft beat drifted down from upstairs. Instead of clashing, the drum pattern matched his tempo. Tural hesitated, then repeated the main chorus a little louder. Upstairs, Emin added a warm synth chord. For fifteen minutes neither of them looked out of the window; they simply listened and answered each other across the courtyard.

Ten minutes later Emin was at the door, holding two cups of iced coffee. “Man, that tar was music to my ears,” he said. “Have you ever tried a collaboration?”

They spent the week running a long cable between the two balconies and practising every evening after six. On Sunday, the neighbours gathered under the mulberry tree in the courtyard for a short live performance. Watching his father fold his arms in the front row, Tural knew it was time to face the music.

They played three pieces. When the last note faded, the courtyard was quiet for a second before breaking into applause. Tural's father cleared his throat. “Well,” he said to Emin, “sometimes an old man has to change your tune — bring your laptop downstairs, my wife made dolma.”

An annoying noise from upstairs turns into a musical partnership that wins over the whole courtyard

To show that he now respects Emin and welcomes him as a neighbour
questions.why: He admits an old man has to change his tune and invites him to eat with the family.

B2.text:
The courtyard on Mirza Fatali Street was built like an amphitheatre: four wooden balconies facing a single mulberry tree, where nobody's life was entirely private. When nineteen-year-old Tural sat by his window to rehearse for his conservatory finals, the neighbours timed their afternoon tea by the scales on his tar.

Peace lasted until June, when Emin moved into the top flat with two studio monitors and a devotion to a genre Tural's father refused to call music at all. Every bass drop rattled the saucer under his tea glass. “The boy is demonstrably tone-deaf,” he announced at dinner. “No melody, no lyrics — just a washing machine with ambitions.”

The truce happened by accident on a stifling Tuesday. Tural was repeating a delicate mugham phrase when a muted electronic pulse began to drift down from above. Rather than drowning him out, it sat underneath his rhythm like a second heartbeat. Curious, Tural leaned toward the balcony rail and played the main chorus twice. Upstairs, an unseen hand wove a warm chord around it. For twenty minutes they traded phrases through the heat, neither daring to break the spell by looking out.

That evening Emin appeared on the landing with a notebook and a sheepish grin. “Look, if my speakers have been driving you mad, I'm sorry,” he said. “But what you played today was music to my ears. Would you consider a collaboration — just fifteen minutes, for the courtyard?”

They strung a cable between the balconies and spent four nights arguing pleasantly over tempos. On Sunday, thirty neighbours pulled chairs under the mulberry tree for the live performance. Seeing his father seated squarely in the middle with his arms crossed, Tural felt his stomach drop: it was time to face the music.

What followed was seven minutes in which a three-hundred-year-old instrument and a laptop sounded as though they had grown up in the same house. When the final note hung in the dusk, Tural's father stood up slowly.

“A stubborn man hates to change your tune,” he said, looking up at Emin's balcony, “so I won't say I was wrong. I'll only say my wife has made qutab, and the tea is getting cold.”

questions.q: What is the central idea of the story?
options: Traditional music is disappearing in modern Baku
An unexpected dialogue between tradition and modern sound bridges a generational divide
Living in old courtyard buildings causes conflicts between neighbours
Conservatory exams are too strict for young musicians
questions.why: A tar player and an electronic producer turn balcony noise into a piece that moves even the sceptical father.

questions.q: How did Tural's father describe Emin's music at dinner?
questions.why: “No melody, no lyrics — just a washing machine with ambitions.”

questions.q: Why did neither Tural nor Emin look out of the window the first time they played together?
options: They were afraid of Tural's father
Neither wanted to break the spell of the moment
They did not know where the sound was coming from
questions.why: “Neither daring to break the spell by looking out.”

questions.q: Emin apologised to Tural in case his speakers had been bothering the family.
questions.why: “Look, if my speakers have been driving you mad, I'm sorry.”

questions.q: Tural's father called Emin “tone-deaf”. What does “tone-deaf” mean?
options: Unable to hear the difference between musical notes
questions.why: He says Emin's music has no melody, like a washing machine.

questions.q: What does Tural's father's final speech show about his character?
options: He is still angry and wants Emin to stop playing
He is too proud to say directly “I was wrong”, so he shows his approval by inviting Emin to eat
He did not actually listen to the performance
questions.why: He says “so I won't say I was wrong” and immediately invites Emin down for qutab and tea.

podcast.title: Singing in front of everyone

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: Do you sing at karaoke? Guess: who in this episode sang at a wedding — Leyla or Sam?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is music — and I have a confession. I'm completely tone-deaf.
[laugh] I know. I heard you at karaoke last month.
Everyone heard me. I chose a slow love song, and by the chorus half the room was laughing.
But you finished it! That was brave. And the next morning you had to face the music — your friend posted the video.
[sigh] Four hundred views. My mum watched it twice.
My story is the opposite. Last summer my cousin asked me to sing at her wedding.
Really? What did you sing?
An old Azerbaijani song with a beautiful melody. I didn't know all the lyrics, so I had to learn them first.
And did you practise a lot?
I had to rehearse every evening for three weeks. My neighbours know that song very well now.
[chuckle] And on the day?
When I finished, my grandmother was crying. She hugged me and said, "That was music to my ears."
That's lovely. A live performance is so different from singing in the shower.
Totally. So what do you listen to, Sam? Which genre is your favourite?
Mostly indie rock. But for years I hated jazz. I said it was just noise. Then a friend took me to a jazz club in London.
And one night made you change your tune?
Completely. Live, jazz is magic. Now I go every month.
My favourite thing right now is a collaboration between two very different artists — like a rapper and an opera singer.
Those are great. Two styles, one song. Sometimes it works, and sometimes it's a disaster.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: what song do you know all the words to — and why?
Please don't ask me to sing it. See you next time!
Bye for now!
